| [LIT-147](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-147.md) v3 | Mental causation via neuroprosthetics? A critical analysis | Pernu (2018), DOI-10.1007/s11229-018-1713-z. The interventionist/difference-making case for nonreductive mental causation from BCIs (List & Menzies 2009; Menzies 2015; Woodward 2008a,b, 2017) misplaces multiple realisation. What the ensemble recordings show is that one cortical-level variable N (the ensemble's average firing) is realised by many single-neuron patterns N1, N2. Each intention M corresponds to one value of N. So the counterfactual contrast "∼M □→ ∼B true, ∼N □→ ∼B false" fails, and neuroprosthetics supports mental causation only by identifying M with N, not nonreductive physicalism. | Active — read in full 2026-09-26 ([NOTE-091](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-091.md)); Worth reading as a short, precise diagnosis of a specific equivocation in the interventionist BCI argument (multiple realisation at the wrong level). The Procrustes shape distance between two representations (optimal rotational alignment of units) equals the Bures distance between their centred linear kernel matrices, so the rotation-invariant geometry of a representation is exactly the geometry of its kernel, and through Uhlmann's theorem the fidelity of two kernels is the maximum overlap over all representations consistent with them. | Active — read 2026-10-14 (NOTE-753) in full; worth reading as the clean finite-dimensional statement that, for centred linear kernels, the Procrustes distance equals the Bures distance and normalized Bures similarity is the cosine of the Riemannian shape distance, so the kernel is a complete invariant of a representation up to translation and orthogonal maps, and as the proof that CKA and NBS are related only within a rank-dependent envelope. Kanerva's SDM read weights each stored pointer by the number of neurons in the intersection of two Hamming balls of radius d. The paper shows that this weight is roughly log-linear in Hamming distance for close patterns. As a result, with L²-normalised vectors and a regression-fitted β, softmax attention reproduces SDM's retrieval behaviour on random and learnt-projection data (App. B.7). Two things are weaker than they look. The analytic derivation (App. B.2, Eqs. 16–21) gets the exponent wrong: by my recomputation its β is ≈2–2.5× too small. | [LIT-368](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-368.md) v2 | A decision-making theory of visual detection | Tanner & Swets (1954), DOI-10.1037/h0058700. Tanner and Swets model visual detection as testing a statistical hypothesis. The observer compares one sample of neural activity with a cutoff, and signal+noise and noise are Gaussian with equal variance, separated by d′ (the mean difference in noise-SD units, defined as the square root of Peterson and Birdsall's d). The cutoff moves along a curve of P_SN(A) against P_N(A) (the curve now called the ROC; for d′ = 1 it passes through (.16, .50), (.50, .84) and (.84, .98)). The optimal operating point is where the slope equals β = [(1−P(SN))/P(SN)]·[(V_N·CA+K_N·A)/(V_SN·A+K_SN·CA)]. The 4AFC prediction is P(C)=∫F(x)³g(x)dx. With three paid observers, d′ estimated from yes-no data predicted 4AFC accuracy. The "false alarms are guesses" (high-threshold) hypothesis is rejected: false-alarm rate correlated with chance-corrected thresholds (ρ = .30, .71, .67; combined p ≪ .001), and all 12 fitted yes-no scatter lines miss the point (1, 1). | Active — read in full 2026-09-30 ([NOTE-316](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-316.md)); worth reading as the founding psychophysics paper of signal detection theory: it is short, it is the first place d′ is named, and it is the first to put the observer on the ROC and to set the likelihood-ratio criterion β from priors and payoffs. For the ideal-observer mathematics it defers entirely to Peterson and Birdsall (1953), and its experiment is small (three observers) with some statistics asserted rather than shown. |
| [LIT-373](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-373.md) v4 | The two dragons of cognition: recursive condensation for predictive processing | Li (2026), DOI-10.3389/fncom.2026.1778902. A "Hypothesis and Theory" essay proposing that the neocortex is a "biological Savitch machine". Alternating expansion ("odd parity") and contraction ("even parity") phases manufacture the disjoint closed sets of Urysohn's Lemma, and storing ("memoizing") the condensed tokens converts exponential search into polynomial "navigation". Its one non-standard formal result, Theorem 2, R(N) ∝ b^{αN} (§5.2.2, p. 11), is stated without proof. There is no data, simulation or model. The two mathematical pillars are misdescribed: Savitch's theorem saves space at the cost of time and does not memoize, and Urysohn's Lemma gives a continuous separator, not a linear one, and is not an "if and only if". | Rejected — re-read jointly with [LIT-374](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-374.md) and arXiv 2602.07974 on 2026-10-01 ([NOTE-321](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-321.md)); Read jointly with [LIT-374](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-374.md) and the companion StrLT preprint (arXiv 2602.07974), the essay is the cognitive motivation of a coherent programme: structure is discovered by costly search, condensed into frozen tokens, and reused cheaply. It is not just a misuse of two theorems. Read charitably, its mathematical slips are repairable and are not the reason to set it aside: the Urysohn "iff" and linear readout, Savitch as memoisation, the Definition 2 clash. The reason is what is left after repair: an amortised-inference and complementary-learning-systems picture already in the literature it cites; a neural mapping whose predictions do not discriminate it from standard consolidation accounts; one original quantitative claim, Theorem 2, that is not argued. A reader who wants the programme should read [LIT-374](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-374.md) and the companion, where it is made precise. |

| [LIT-384](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-384.md) | The somatic marker hypothesis and the possible functions of the prefrontal cortex | Damasio (1996), DOI-10.1098/rstb.1996.0125. States the somatic marker hypothesis: ventromedial prefrontal cortex holds learned links between classes of situation and the body states (emotions) that went with them; when a situation recurs, those states are re-enacted, through the body or through an "as if" loop in somatosensory cortex, and mark imagined option-outcome pairs as good or bad, overtly as a feeling or covertly as a bias, so that reasoning works over a pruned space. Evidence summarised: ventromedial patients with intact intellect decide badly in life, lack skin-conductance responses to emotive pictures, and in the gambling task keep choosing the losing decks and show no anticipatory responses. | Active — read in full 2026-10-01 ([NOTE-332](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-332.md)); worth reading as the shortest statement of the somatic marker hypothesis by its author, with the evidence it then rested on. It is a hypothesis paper: the mechanism (ventromedial prefrontal linkages that re-enact body states, by a "body loop" or an "as if body loop", which then mark options good or bad) is stated, not shown, and the evidence it reports is lesion and skin-conductance work summarised from other papers, without numbers. Its strongest piece, that ventromedial patients lack anticipatory skin-conductance responses in the gambling task while responding normally to the losses themselves, is reported here in one paragraph; the 1997 Science report filed alongside it is the place to see that result. Whether the account is true is not this note's question. |

| [LIT-431](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-431.md) | Time and the Observer: The Where and When of Consciousness in the Brain | Dennett & Kinsbourne (1992), Behavioral and Brain Sciences 15(2):183–201, with open peer commentary. There is no place in the brain where "it all comes together" for consciousness. Discriminations are made once, locally, and revised in parallel "drafts", none canonical. The brain represents temporal order by content, not by the timing of its own vehicles, as a dated letter does. Colour phi, the cutaneous rabbit and Libet's timing results stop looking anomalous. Whether a revision was pre-experiential (Stalinesque) or post-experiential (Orwellian) has no answer at that scale. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-367](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-367.md)), the target article only; worth reading as the shortest complete statement of the Multiple Drafts model and of the case against "Cartesian materialism", worked out on four timing phenomena (colour phi, the cutaneous rabbit, Libet's backward referral and his delayed intention). Its sound core is the distinction between the time a content is represented and the time it represents. Its strong claim, that the Orwellian/Stalinesque distinction "need have no answer" below a few hundred milliseconds, is an argument from indistinguishability, not a demonstration. The open peer commentary (pp. 201–247) was not read. |
| [LIT-445](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-445.md) | From the Phenomenology to the Mechanisms of Consciousness: Integrated Information Theory 3.0 | Oizumi, Albantakis & Tononi (2014), PLoS Computational Biology 10(5):e1003588. IIT 3.0 states five axioms of experience (existence, composition, information, integration, exclusion), turns each into a postulate about mechanisms in a state, and identifies an experience with the maximally irreducible conceptual structure of a "complex". Exclusion makes a complex a local maximum of integrated conceptual information Φ over all overlapping sets of elements, so complexes cannot overlap and no subset or superset of a complex is conscious. Worked logic-gate examples show minor complexes beside a major one, an inactive network that is conscious, a minimally conscious photodiode, and a feed-forward "zombie" functionally equivalent to a conscious system. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-365](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-365.md)), equations excepted; worth reading as the formal statement of the exclusion postulate that Schwitzgebel's 2014 manuscript ([LIT-159](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-159.md)) attacks: "of all overlapping sets of elements, only one set can be conscious", a complex being a local maximum of Φ against every overlapping set. It is IIT's anti-nesting principle, stated as a postulate and motivated only by the phenomenological exclusion axiom; the paper's Occam's-razor argument is given for exclusion within a mechanism, not between systems. It also says plainly that function does not fix consciousness, which is IIT's answer to whether agency built from parts brings experience with it. |
| [LIT-450](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-450.md) | Self models | Metzinger (2007, rev. 2013), Scholarpedia 2(10):4174. There is no substantial self, only a phenomenal self-model (PSM): the conscious part of an organism's self-model, an instrument of global control. A phenomenal self arises "if and only if a system operates under a transparent PSM", one it cannot introspectively recognise as a model; a first-person perspective is a transparent model of the intentionality relation (PMIR). Self-models can be unconscious and artificial, as in Bongard, Zykov and Lipson's limping starfish robot; embodiment comes in three orders, the third conscious. Full-body illusions are offered as the experimental handle. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-372](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-372.md)); worth reading as Metzinger's own short, open statement of the self-model theory of subjectivity (SMT) behind Being No One ([LIT-467](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-467.md)): there is no self, only a phenomenal self-model, and a system experiences itself as a self when that model is transparent, that is, when it cannot introspectively recognise it as a model. It is an encyclopedia article, not an argument: the central claim is stated as a definition with a prediction attached, its empirical examples are cited, and the online text is a revision later than the 2007 acceptance, with editing slips. |
| [LIT-453](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-453.md) | Philosophical conceptions of the self: implications for cognitive science | Gallagher (2000), Trends in Cognitive Sciences 4(1):14–21. Divides philosophical accounts of the self into the "minimal self", accessible to present self-consciousness without temporal extension, and the "narrative self", extended in time through memory and story. The minimal self splits into a sense of ownership and a sense of agency, which come apart in involuntary movement and, after Frith, in schizophrenic thought insertion when a forward comparator fails. Neonatal imitation suggests an embodied minimal self; Strawson's and Tani's are momentary. Against Dennett's narrative centre, the self is "the sum total of its narratives". Read in the author's preprint. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-377](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-377.md)), in the author's preprint, not the typeset article; worth reading as the paper that set the minimal self against the narrative self for cognitive science, and for the split of the minimal self into a sense of ownership and a sense of agency, which it ties to Frith's comparator model of schizophrenic thought insertion. It is a short review: the empirical support is cited, not shown, and its own proposal, the self as "the sum total of its narratives", is offered in two paragraphs. |
| [LIT-467](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-467.md) v3 | Being No One: The Self-Model Theory of Subjectivity | Metzinger (2003), MIT Press. Per its publisher, "no such things as selves exist in the world: nobody ever had or was a self. All that exists are phenomenal selves", and the phenomenal self is "the content of a 'transparent self-model'". A representationalist and functional analysis of the conscious first-person perspective, with conceptual "tools", constraints on consciousness and neurophenomenological case studies (agnosia, neglect, blindsight, hallucination), asking whether being someone can be analysed at subpersonal levels. Unread: registered from the description and the contents; the theory is read in [LIT-450](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-450.md). | Unavailable — registered 2026-10-02 from the publisher's description and the chapter list on Crossref, not read: no lawful full text of the book could be reached. The MIT Press Direct edition is not open access and no author copy is posted. Its theory is read in Metzinger's own short statement, "Self models" ([LIT-450](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-450.md), read in full), and more fully in his "Précis: Being No One" (PSYCHE 11(5), 2005; LIT-568, read in full 2026-10-03), the read substitute for the book, which sets out six of its ten constraints and the phenomenal model of the intentionality relation. Retried 2026-11-01: OpenAlex still reports it closed with no open location; it is not in the Internet Archive's MIT Press open-access collection, which holds Metzinger's 2024 book (LIT-1943); MIT Press Direct returned a Cloudflare challenge; no author copy found. It stays Unavailable until a copy is supplied, not on merit. |
| [LIT-540](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-540.md) | Impulsive action: emotional impulses and their control | Frijda, Ridderinkhof & Rietveld (2014), Frontiers in Psychology 5:518. Impulsive action is non-deliberate but purposive. Automatic appraisal of an event's pertinence to the agent's concerns elicits a state of action readiness, a motive to establish, modify or end a relation to the object, with "control precedence" (urgency, persistence, attentional capture). Modes of action readiness are what distinguish one emotion from another. Events usually draw several appraisals and so several states of readiness, and their interaction regulates action: much emotion regulation is itself emotional, not reason overriding passion. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-433](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-433.md)); filed in place of Frijda's The Emotions ([LIT-546](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-546.md)), which could not be read, as the shortest lawfully readable statement of his action-readiness theory in his own words. Appraisal of an event's pertinence to one's concerns elicits a state of action readiness, a motive to change one's relation to the object, which has "control precedence". Modes of action readiness correspond to emotions (hostility to anger, avoidance to fear). Much emotion regulation is itself one state of action readiness checking another, so "there is no clear distinction between processes of emotion and processes of emotion regulation". It is a theoretical paper with no data, written for impulsive action, so it states the theory's core and not its full range. |
| [LIT-542](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-542.md) | The theory of constructed emotion: an active inference account of interoception and categorization | Barrett (2017), SCAN 12(1):1–23. The brain runs an internal model of the body in the world for allostasis. Its predictions are "concepts" issued from agranular limbic cortex and refined by prediction error. Interoceptive predictions are felt as affect (valence, arousal). An emotion is an instance of categorizing sensation with an emotion concept, built the same way as any perception. Since instances of an emotion are "created by multiple spatiotemporal patterns" (degeneracy), the categories have no neural essences, and the classical view, basic-emotion and causal appraisal theories included, is rejected. Emotions are "constructions of the world, not reactions to it." | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-434](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-434.md)); worth reading as the shortest complete statement of the theory of constructed emotion and of its link to predictive processing. The brain's core task is allostasis, run through an internal model whose predictions are "concepts". An instance of emotion is what happens when the brain categorizes predicted interoceptive and exteroceptive sensation with an emotion concept. On this account emotion categories have no neural "essences", and causal appraisal theories are "highly doubtful". The paper is a theoretical synthesis: its own data are a few figures, and the rest is cited evidence and explicitly labelled hypotheses. |
| [LIT-563](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-563.md) | HDDM: Hierarchical Bayesian Estimation of the Drift-Diffusion Model in Python | Wiecki, Sofer & Frank (2013), Frontiers in Neuroinformatics 7:14. HDDM is an open-source Python package that estimates the drift diffusion model (and the linear ballistic accumulator) by hierarchical Bayesian MCMC: subject parameters drawn from group distributions with informative priors, full posteriors, outlier handling, and regression of parameters on trial-by-trial covariates. A tutorial reproduces a theta-power effect on decision threshold that reverses under subthalamic deep brain stimulation. In simulations hierarchical Bayes recovers parameters and detects effects better than χ²-quantile and maximum-likelihood fitting, most with few trials. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-466](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-466.md)); worth reading as the methods paper for HDDM, the Python package that fits the drift diffusion model by hierarchical Bayesian estimation (PyMC, MCMC), with subject parameters drawn from group distributions and trial-by-trial regressions of parameters on covariates such as EEG power. Its simulations show hierarchical Bayes recovering parameters with less error than per-subject χ²-quantile, maximum-likelihood or non-hierarchical Bayesian fits, most of all with few trials, and detecting drift-rate differences and covariate effects more often. The comparisons are the authors' own, on data simulated from the model being fitted, and its hypothesis tests on the group posterior differ from the t-tests used for the other methods. |
| [LIT-565](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-565.md) | The Time Course of Perceptual Choice: The Leaky, Competing Accumulator Model | Usher & McClelland (2001), Psychological Review 108(3):550–592. Perceptual choice as gradual, stochastic accumulation in one unit per alternative, with leakage and lateral inhibition between units and a threshold at zero. For two choices the linearised difference is an Ornstein–Uhlenbeck process with net leak K = k − β; K = 0 recovers the classical diffusion model, and K ≠ 0 bounds asymptotic accuracy. The model fits time–accuracy curves slightly better than diffusion with drift variance, fits Vickers's latency–discriminability data, predicts individual primacy or recency biases confirmed in a new experiment, and yields Hick's law under a constant-accuracy criterion. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-449](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-449.md)); worth reading as the source of the leaky, competing accumulator (LCA): one leaky accumulator per alternative, lateral inhibition between them, a threshold-linear floor at zero, and an absolute response criterion. In the linear two-choice case the difference between accumulators is an Ornstein–Uhlenbeck process with net leak K = k − β, so the classical diffusion model is the special case K = 0 and accuracy given unlimited time is bounded whenever K ≠ 0. Its evidence for leakage over drift variance is a modest likelihood advantage on 3 participants (combined ratio about 62 to 1, 7 of 9 curves), and the authors concede that a diffusion model with drift variance, starting-point variance and decision boundaries is hard to tell apart from it. |
| [LIT-568](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-568.md) | Précis: Being No One | Metzinger (2005), PSYCHE 11(5), the author's précis of Being No One. Minimal consciousness is a global world-model in a window of presence that cannot be recognised as a model (globality, presentationality, transparency). A phenomenal self is a transparent self-model: "no such things as selves exist in the world". Transparency comes in degrees, and the self-model's opaque partition is what lets humans doubt their own self-representation. The unity of consciousness is a single global functional cluster. A first-person perspective is a phenomenal model of the intentionality relation, and iterating it yields introspective and social intelligence. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-460](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-460.md)), as the read substitute for Being No One ([LIT-467](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-467.md)), which it summarises in Metzinger's own words. Worth reading as the most complete short statement of the self-model theory of subjectivity (SMT): more of the machinery than "Self models" ([LIT-450](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-450.md)), in particular the six constraints, the degrees of transparency, and the phenomenal model of the intentionality relation (PMIR). Phenomenal selfhood is a transparent self-model, "a function realized by a lack of information"; "no such things as selves exist in the world". The unity of a conscious world is a global functional cluster bound by "highest-order binding". It states the theory and its predictions; the evidence is cited, not shown, and the neural sections say how little is known. |
| [LIT-569](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-569.md) | The Physics of Optimal Decision Making: A Formal Analysis of Models of Performance in Two-Alternative Forced-Choice Tasks | Bogacz, Brown, Moehlis, Holmes & Cohen (2006), Psychological Review 113(4):700–765. The pure drift diffusion model implements the SPRT and Neyman–Pearson test, so it is the optimal two-choice decision process. The O-U, mutual inhibition (Usher–McClelland), feedforward inhibition and pooled inhibition (Wang) models reduce to it for balanced parameters; the race model does not. For reward rate, Bayes risk and two accuracy-weighted criteria there is a unique optimal threshold, giving parameter-free optimal performance curves. With biased priors the optimal starting point is proportional to the log prior odds. | Active — read 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-461](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-461.md)), main text and Appendix B in full, Appendix A (the derivations) by section only; worth reading as the paper that puts the two-choice decision models in one frame and ties them to the sequential probability ratio test. The pure drift diffusion model is the continuum limit of the SPRT, so it is the fastest for a given accuracy and the most accurate for a given time. Of six models, all but the race model reduce to it in some parameter range: the Usher–McClelland mutual inhibition model when leak equals inhibition and both are large, the feedforward inhibition model when its inhibitory and excitatory weights are equal. Each reward criterion has a unique optimal threshold, which gives testable optimal performance curves. The optimality results hold for the pure model with stationary evidence and two alternatives. |
| [LIT-576](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-576.md) | The Diffusion Decision Model: Theory and Data for Two-Choice Decision Tasks | Ratcliff & McKoon (2008), Neural Computation 20(4):873–922. A review of the diffusion decision model for fast two-choice tasks, with three new motion-discrimination experiments. Noisy evidence accumulates from a starting point z to one of two boundaries (0, a) at drift v, plus non-decision time and across-trial variability in v, z and Ter. The model fits accuracy and full correct and error RT distributions, and maps difficulty to drift, speed–accuracy instructions to boundary separation and stimulus proportion mainly to starting point. Applications cover aging, aphasia and links to neural firing. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-445](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-445.md)), from the author manuscript in PubMed Central; worth reading as the canonical statement of the diffusion decision model and of what it is for. Two-choice RT and accuracy are decomposed into drift rate (quality of evidence), boundary separation (caution), starting point (bias) and non-decision time, plus across-trial variability in drift, starting point and non-decision time. Three new motion-discrimination experiments show each manipulation landing on its own parameter: difficulty on drift, speed–accuracy instructions on boundaries, stimulus proportion mainly on starting point. Its closing claim, that diffusion models have come "as near to provid[ing] a solution to simple decision making as is possible in behavioral science", is the authors' assessment, not a result. |
| [LIT-578](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-578.md) v2 | Dynamic Patterns: The Self-Organization of Brain and Behavior | Kelso (1995), Dynamic Patterns: The Self-Organization of Brain and Behavior, MIT Press, xvii + 334 pp. The book-length statement of coordination dynamics. Unread: registered from catalogue records. What the record knows of its content comes from the works that cite it: the coordination potential of the HKB model (reproduced in Kelso 2021, Box 1), absolute versus relative coordination (De Jaegher & Di Paolo 2007, citing p. 98), a chapter on how HKB arose (ch. 3) and one on brain rhythms (ch. 8), per Kelso 2021. | Unavailable — registered 2026-10-03 as a seed, not read. No lawful full text was found: the book has no DOI, is not listed as open access, and MIT Press's page refused an automated request. Under the owner's rule for books it is supplanted by a shorter work by the same author, Kelso's 2021 retrospective on the HKB model ([LIT-601](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-601.md)), which was read. It is filed because it is the citation others reach for when they mean coordination dynamics, relative coordination or metastability; De Jaegher & Di Paolo ([LIT-571](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-571.md)) and Raja et al. ([LIT-598](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-598.md)) both cite it. |
| [LIT-580](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-580.md) | Uncertainty-based competition between prefrontal and dorsolateral striatal systems for behavioral control | Daw, Niv & Dayan (2005), Nature Neuroscience 8(12):1704-1711. Habitual and goal-directed control are model-free ("caching") and model-based ("tree-search") reinforcement learners in dorsolateral striatum and prefrontal cortex. Behaviour follows whichever controller's value estimate is less uncertain under approximate Bayesian versions of each. Simulations reproduce the devaluation data: over-training yields devaluation-insensitive habit, except for actions near reward or in tasks with more actions and outcomes. Both controllers serve the same ends; neither is the "irrational" one. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-459](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-459.md)), supplementary methods not read. Worth reading as the founding statement of model-based versus model-free control as two brain systems, and of arbitration between them by relative uncertainty. Goal-directed (devaluation-sensitive) behaviour is a prefrontal "tree-search" controller, statistically efficient but noisy to compute. Habit is a dorsolateral-striatal "caching" controller, cheap but data-hungry and blind to revaluation. Each controls behaviour when its value estimate is the more certain, which reproduces why over-training produces habits unless the task is complex or the action near the reward. Both controllers pursue "identical rational ends": a rejection of the impulsive-limbic-versus-rational-prefrontal picture. |
| [LIT-581](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-581.md) | Hierarchically organized behavior and its neural foundations: A reinforcement learning perspective | Botvinick, Niv & Barto (2009), Cognition 113(3):262-280. Hierarchical RL groups actions into reusable "options" with their own policies, subgoals and pseudo-reward. That eases the scaling problem by cutting the number of decisions to explore and learn. The paper builds an actor-critic version and maps option identifiers to DLPFC, option-specific policies to dorsolateral striatum, and option-specific values and option-length prediction errors to OFC. Unsuitable options produce negative transfer, so how useful options are discovered is the central open problem. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-451](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-451.md)), from the PubMed Central author manuscript; the online appendix with the equations was not read. Worth reading as the bridge between hierarchical reinforcement learning (temporally abstract "options") and the psychology and neuroscience of hierarchically organized behaviour. Options ease the scaling problem of RL by shrinking search and learning to a few decision points. An actor-critic version maps option identifiers to dorsolateral PFC, option-specific policies to dorsolateral striatum, and option-specific values and extended prediction errors to orbitofrontal cortex. The problem it puts first is option discovery: the wrong options cause negative transfer, as in human problem solving. |
| [LIT-584](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-584.md) | Model-based and model-free Pavlovian reward learning: Revaluation, revision, and revelation | Dayan & Berridge (2014), Cognitive, Affective, & Behavioral Neuroscience 14(2):473-492. Pavlovian prediction is not only model-free. A cue that had predicted disgusting salt became instantly "wanted" when a never-experienced salt appetite was induced, before the salt was retasted, which needs a prediction of the outcome's identity revalued against the current bodily state. Over-training may "defocus" outcome representations rather than hand control to a model-free system. Dopamine may carry model-based evaluations. No algorithm for the revaluation is given. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-463](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-463.md)), from the PubMed Central author manuscript. Worth reading as the argument that Pavlovian prediction, usually modelled as purely model-free, is also model-based. In the "Dead Sea salt" experiment a lever that had predicted a disgusting salt solution became, on first presentation after a novel sodium appetite was induced and before any salt was retasted, nearly as attractive as a sucrose lever, with mesolimbic activation. A cached value cannot do that. The CS must predict the outcome's identity, and its value must be recomputed against the current bodily state. The paper adds "defocusing" of outcome representations as a model-based route to apparent habit, and argues that dopamine can carry model-based evaluations. |
| [LIT-585](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-585.md) | The Expected Value of Control: An Integrative Theory of Anterior Cingulate Cortex Function | Shenhav, Botvinick & Cohen (2013), Neuron 79(2):217-240. Control is allocated by a cost-benefit decision. The expected value of control (EVC) of a candidate control signal is its probability-weighted payoff, with future value discounted, minus an intrinsic cost rising with its intensity. dACC monitors state and outcome information and specifies the identity and intensity of the EVC-maximizing signal. Lateral PFC and subcortical structures implement it. The account integrates conflict monitoring, effort costs and the override of defaults (exploration, foraging, patience). | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-446](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-446.md)), from the PubMed Central author manuscript. Worth reading as the standard statement that cognitive control is allocated by a cost-benefit decision. The "expected value of control" (EVC) of a control signal, which has an identity (which task) and an intensity (how much), is its expected payoff minus an intrinsic cost that rises with intensity. Dorsal anterior cingulate cortex is proposed to monitor and to specify the EVC-maximizing signal, which lateral PFC and subcortical structures then implement. It is a review and synthesis: the model is stated, not fitted, and the authors say the ingredients are not new. |
| [LIT-601](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-601.md) | The Haken–Kelso–Bunz (HKB) model: from matter to movement to mind | Kelso (2021), Biological Cybernetics 115(4):305–322, a 60th-anniversary retrospective. HKB models bimanual coordination by the relative phase φ, with dφ/dt = −a sin φ − 2b sin 2φ and potential V = −a cos φ − b cos 2φ: both in-phase and anti-phase are stable for b/a > 1/4, and anti-phase loses stability below it, as observed when movement frequency rises. Noise, symmetry breaking (Δω) and metastability extend it; with Kuramoto's model it becomes a generalized HKB for many agents. The same dynamics is reported within a body, between people and with machines, and in brain activity. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-467](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-467.md)), from the free-to-read publisher PDF. Filed in place of Kelso's book Dynamic Patterns ([LIT-578](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-578.md)) and as the read account of the paywalled Haken–Kelso–Bunz paper ([LIT-588](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-588.md)), both Deferred. Worth reading as Kelso's own short statement of coordination dynamics: the HKB order-parameter equation for relative phase, its stochastic and symmetry-breaking extensions, metastability as relative coordination, the generalized HKB–Kuramoto model, and the claim that one coordination dynamics holds within and between people. It is a retrospective by an author of the model, not a review, and it says so. |
| [LIT-605](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-605.md) | An Accumulator Model for Spontaneous Neural Activity Prior to Self-Initiated Movement | Schurger, Sitt & Dehaene (2012), PNAS 109(42). In Libet's spontaneous movement task, a leaky stochastic accumulator, δx = (I − kx)Δt + cξ√Δt, with weak constant urgency I and a threshold, fitted only to waiting times, reproduces the averaged readiness potential (r² = 0.96): time-locking to threshold crossings averages up the autocorrelated noise that produced them. Fast responses to random interruptions were preceded by a slow negativity, as predicted. The "neural decision to move now" is the late threshold crossing, about 150 ms before movement, so Libet's inference of an unconscious decision a half-second earlier is unfounded. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-462](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-462.md)); worth reading as the model that reinterprets the readiness potential. A leaky stochastic accumulator with a weak constant input ("urgency"), fitted with three parameters to 14 participants' waiting times in Libet's task, reproduces the shape of the averaged readiness potential (r² = 0.96) because averaging epochs time-locked to threshold crossings recovers the noise that happened to carry the accumulator there. Its prediction, that fast responses to unpredictable clicks are preceded by a slow negativity, was confirmed (13 participants). On this account the "neural decision to move now" is the threshold crossing about 150 ms before movement, not the onset of the readiness potential, and Libet's inference that the brain decides before awareness is "unfounded". The authors say plainly that this shows the readiness potential could reflect spontaneous fluctuation, not that it does. |
| [LIT-614](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-614.md) | Bayesian model reduction | Friston, Parr & Zeidman (2018; v2 2019), arXiv:1805.07092. A review of Bayesian model reduction: given a fitted full model's prior P, approximate posterior Q and free energy F, the free energy of a model with any other prior P̃ is ln E_Q[P̃/P] + F, and its posterior follows by reweighting Q (Eqs. 9–10). Closed forms are given for Gaussian, Dirichlet, beta, gamma, categorical and multinomial priors. Three worked simulations (sparse regression, cluster pruning in a Gaussian mixture, network discovery in a linear dynamical system) and a review of uses: structure learning, hierarchical (PEB) inversion as a cascade of reductions, and "sleep-like" pruning in active-inference agents. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-477](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-477.md)); worth reading as the reference statement of Bayesian model reduction (BMR): the reduced free energy F[P̃:P] ≈ ln E_Q[P̃/P] + F[P] (Eq. 9), which the authors call a generalisation of the Savage–Dickey ratio "to any new prior", with closed forms for Gaussian, Dirichlet, beta, gamma, categorical and multinomial priors (Eqs. 11–12, Table 1). The Dirichlet form is what lets active-inference agents prune their own likelihood mappings. Its examples are simulations, and its review of applications is of the authors' own lab. |
| [LIT-615](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-615.md) | An Active Inference Approach to Modeling Structure Learning: Concept Learning as an Example Case | Smith, Schwartenbeck, Parr & Friston (2020), Front. Comput. Neurosci. 14:41. A partially observed Markov decision process with eight animal "slots", some starting with flat likelihoods, learns new concepts without feedback: a slot is engaged only when its flat mapping explains a feature combination better than any learned concept. Bayesian model reduction on the learned prior over states then resets slots the data did not need. In 100 runs per condition the true number of concepts won in 45–80% of runs for 4–7 concepts and rarely for 2–3, and in every run when the likelihood was given. The agent also generalises to an unseen animal in one shot, and the paper simulates neural and dopaminergic responses. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-485](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-485.md)); worth reading as the record's worked example of structure learning in an active-inference agent: "model expansion" by spare hidden-state slots whose flat likelihoods win inference only for a truly novel stimulus, and "model reduction" by applying Bayesian model reduction to the agent's learned prior over states, so that unused slots are reset. It is a proof of concept with eight animals and six features. Reduction recovered the true number of concepts in 45–80% of 100 runs for 4–7 concepts, failed for 2–3, and succeeded every time only when the likelihood mapping was given rather than learned. |
| [LIT-620](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-620.md) | Post hoc Bayesian model selection | Friston & Penny (2011), NeuroImage 56(4):2089–2099. If every model of interest is a full model with a different prior and the same likelihood, the evidence of any reduced model is p(y\|m_F) times the full posterior expectation of p(θ\|m_i)/p(θ\|m_F) (Eq. 3). So the reduced models never have to be fitted. A point-mass reduced prior gives the Savage–Dickey ratio (Eq. 6). Under Gaussian priors and posteriors the reduced free energy and posterior are closed-form in the full model's means and precisions (Eq. 9). In simulations an exhaustive search over 4,096 linear models finds the four true regressors, and 64 network models find the true three-connection graph. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-487](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-487.md)); worth reading as the source of Bayesian model reduction: if a set of models differ from a full model only in their priors, the evidence of each is the full model's evidence times the posterior expectation of the prior ratio (Eq. 3), so one inversion scores them all. Under Gaussian (Laplace) posteriors the reduced free energy is closed-form (Eq. 9). The Savage–Dickey ratio is the point-mass special case (Eq. 6), and ARD and model selection are the same evidence maximisation over prior hyperparameters. The demonstrations are simulations, and whether the reduced free energy of a nonlinear model is a good proxy for the free energy of the reduced model is left open by the authors. |
| [LIT-626](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-626.md) | Three types of phenomenal consciousness and their functional roles: unfolding the ALARM theory of consciousness | Newen & Montemayor (2025), Phil. Basic arousal, realisable without cortex, alarms the body when a homeostatic variable leaves its tolerance range, overriding slow regulation with no choice involved; it adds lasting care for the injury and one-shot, generalised avoidance learning. General alertness, cortical and attention-guided, enables flexible learning and decision-making. Reflexive self-consciousness is general alertness with metacognitive self-relational content, not a third kind of experience, and enables long-term planning that accounts for one's own and others' mindsets. Consciousness occurs when mind contents are spontaneously identified as belonging to their organism, and a continuous flow of homeostatic feelings (hunger, pain, well-being, plain feelings of existence) supplies that identification and "lends" consciousness to exteroceptive images. Feelings are hybrid: interoceptive pathways are unmyelinated, partly non-synaptic and unprotected by a blood–brain barrier, so the body and its neural map interact directly. Posterior brainstem lesions abolish consciousness where large cortical ones may not; consciousness needs "a partnership of nervous systems with the bodies they serve". | Active — skimmed 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-507](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-507.md)): every section was covered, but through a fetch tool that returned section-by-section accounts with short quotes, not a verbatim copy, so the quotes are unchecked; worth reading as the shortest complete statement of the Damasios' claim that consciousness is the spontaneous identification of mind contents as one's own, supplied by a continuous flow of homeostatic feelings, which are hybrid: in interoception the map and the body it maps interact and "commingle". It is a five-page Essay with no data. Its evidence is clinical and cited (brainstem coma versus cortical lesions, general anaesthesia), and its mechanism is the cellular contrast in Table 1: unmyelinated, non-synaptic, barrier-free interoceptive pathways. |

Only the biological theory fully acknowledges the explanatory gap; the others replace it with a puzzle their own theory creates. Concept dualism stops the gap becoming dualism. In four natural odour sources the rank order of correlations between compound concentrations has the clique-topology signature of points near the surface of a 3D hyperbolic ball and not of a uniform Euclidean cube, and human perceptual descriptions of 127 odorants have that of a full 3D hyperbolic ball. Pleasantness, boiling point and acidity read out as linear axes of the fitted fruit-odour space. For four natural odour sources (strawberry, tomato, blueberry, mouse urine; 45–78 compounds over 50–101 samples), the rank order of absolute concentration correlations gives Betti curves that match points sampled near the surface of a 3D hyperbolic ball (R_max = 7, R_min = 0.9 R_max, the same for all four) and reject uniform Euclidean cubes of any dimension tried. Human descriptor profiles for 127 odorants (Dravnieks) match a full 3D hyperbolic ball and no Euclidean cube. | [LIT-875](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-875.md) | An argument for hyperbolic geometry in neural circuits | Sharpee (2019 online), Curr. Opin. Neurobiol. 58:101–104. A four-page review arguing that neural and other biological circuits should have hyperbolic geometry, because hyperbolic space approximates trees, hyperbolic networks are navigable, and Zipf's law, read as states growing exponentially with log-improbability and taken as the mark of maximally informative, latent-driven systems, shares that exponential growth. Its evidence is the olfactory embedding of Zhou, Smith & Sharpee (2018) and earlier perception work; the Zipf-to-hyperbolic link is an analogy, not a derivation. | Active — read 2026-10-09 ([NOTE-670](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-670.md)); worth reading as the short programmatic statement, by the lab behind the olfactory and hippocampal hyperbolic findings, of why hyperbolic geometry should be expected in neural circuits, and as a map of the literatures it joins: hyperbolic random graphs and greedy routing, Zipf's law and statistical criticality, and maximally informative representations. Its own argument is a chain of analogies, not a derivation. Zipf's law is rewritten as a count of states growing exponentially with energy (−log probability), and exponential growth of states is a hallmark of trees and of hyperbolic space, so the two are said to be connected; but exponential growth of states holds for any system with extensive entropy, and what singles out Zipf (unit slope) plays no part in the step to geometry. A rigidity argument for three dimensions cites Mostow's theorem, which concerns finite-volume hyperbolic manifolds of every dimension ≥ 3 and says nothing about point clouds. The one piece of data, a 3D Poincaré-ball embedding of fruit odorants with a pleasantness gradient, is reproduced from Zhou, Smith & Sharpee (2018). |

The pairwise correlations of rat dorsal CA1 place cells have the topological signature of points sampled uniformly from a three-dimensional hyperbolic ball, not of a low-dimensional Euclidean cube, and the ball's radius grows with the logarithm of exploration time. The fitted radius (10.5–15.5 in units of inverse curvature) grows with the logarithm of exploration time, on scales from seconds to days, as the maximal information acquirable does. Place-field sizes are close to exponential, as the model requires, and in simulation exponentially distributed field sizes give more Fisher information than uniform or log-normal ones, with an optimal radius growing as log N that extrapolates to the radius measured. The "hierarchy" is one of nested place-field sizes; no tree is recovered from the data, and the only null geometry tested is Euclidean with uniform sampling. |

Read it knowing that every number in it (the 0.15N capacity, the basin width, the fusion of memories closer than about a tenth of N, the loss of all memories under overload) comes from simulations at N = 30 and 100, and that its "stable states of no obvious meaning" appear at a low load, not only past capacity. |

| [LIT-949](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-949.md) v2 | A synergistic workspace for human consciousness revealed by Integrated Information Decomposition | Luppi et al. (2024), eLife 12:RP88173. Pairwise synergy and redundancy between 454 regions of resting-state fMRI (HCP, N = 100), from Gaussian integrated information decomposition, define a "synergistic workspace". The rest are broadcasters, mainly in the executive control network with lateral prefrontal cortex. Across propofol anaesthesia (against wakefulness and against recovery) and 22 patients with disorders of consciousness, revised integrated information ΦR falls consistently between default-mode gateway regions. The original whole-minus-sum Φ shows no common fall, and the increases near broadcasters are not robust. The evidence is correlational, pairwise and content-free. | Active — read 2026-10-14 ([NOTE-799](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-799.md)) in full; worth reading as an information-theoretic operationalisation of a global workspace with distinct input and output sides. Pairwise integrated information ΦR falls between default-mode gateways under propofol and in disorders of consciousness, where the original Φ shows no common fall. Read it knowing four things. The two-sided split is imposed by the method, and only where its classes fall is measured. | [LIT-1055](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1055.md) | Contributions of ideal observer theory to vision research | Geisler (2011), Vision Research 51(7). A short review, not a methods paper. It defines the ideal observer as the device that "performs a given task at the optimal level possible, given the available information and any specified constraints", writes the Bayesian ideal as an argmax of expected utility over the posterior given either the stimulus S or a constrained neural representation Z = g(S;θ) (eq. 1), and surveys applications from photon-noise detection to eye-movement search. It gives no formula for efficiency and no procedure for locating information loss beyond saying that constraints are added to the ideal one at a time (optics, receptor sampling, receptor noise, ganglion-cell summation) and that models are built by "degrading the ideal observer with hypothesized neural noise or with hypothesized heuristic computations". Worth reading as a compact statement of Bayesian ideal observer analysis: the ideal is optimal "given the available information and any specified constraints", written as an expected-utility argmax over the posterior given either the stimulus or a constrained neural representation Z = g(S;θ), with a survey of applications and some numbers (r = 0.83 for colour naming on individual cone mosaics; 42% lower MSE for a natural-statistics decoder of peripheral samples; about 99% of variance in contour-occlusion judgments). Its nearest analogue to a bounded class is the comparison with named heuristic rules (serial one-location attention, MAP fixation selection), and its remark that far-below-ideal performance leaves many models standing is the empirical form of the point that a gap does not identify its cause. At about a third of a second, the time scale of a saccade, the article models fixation as a pointer that binds a variable in a behavioural program to a place in the world, so that what is bound is only the task-relevant feature, fetched just before use. In a block-copying task subjects looked back at the model about 1.3 times per block on average, the commonest cycle being two looks per block (one apparently for colour, one for position), and chose this slowest, lowest-memory strategy (about 3 s a block, against about 1.5 s for copying from memory) though told to be fast; separating model and copy by 70° cut looks to 1.0 per block, and one-colour patterns that could be chunked cut them to 0.7. The authors read this as working memory having a "carrying cost" that exceeds the cost of re-acquiring from the world, but that cost is inferred from the choices and never measured or modelled, and the evidence is one task with small samples (seven subjects for the main data, three for the colour-change experiment) and no statistics reported in the article. What is left in the world is unprocessed input, not a computed result, and the article argues against precomputation where the needed products cannot be foreseen. | Active — read in full 2026-10-15 (the target article, pp. 723–742; the open peer commentaries and the authors' response, pp. 742–767, not read) from the typeset BBS PDF posted on Dana Ballard's University of Texas page (www.cs.utexas.edu/~dana/bbs.pdf; the same file is on Rajesh Rao's University of Washington page). Unpaywall and OpenAlex report the DOI closed. Worth reading as the founding statement of fixation as a pointer that binds a program variable to a place in the world at about a third of a second, and for the block-copying evidence that people re-look rather than memorize: about 1.3 looks at the model per block, the slowest lowest-memory strategy (about 3 s a block, against 1.5 s from memory) chosen most often under instructions to be fast, falling to 1.0 when looking is made dearer (70° separation) and 0.7 when patterns can be chunked. For [QUESTION-095](../../../record/questions.d/QUESTION-095.md) it shows the trade stated as a cost comparison ("carrying cost" of working memory against on-line acquisition) that moves with both costs, but the cost is inferred from choice, not measured or modelled, what is left in the world is raw input rather than a computed result, and the authors argue against precomputing where needs are unpredictable, so it is the deferral policy opposite to the cockpit's, not amortization; for [TERM-055](../../../record/terms.d/TERM-055.md) it shows people choosing between internal and external sources by their relative retrieval cost, and moving retrieval later, not earlier; for [CLAIM-298](../../../record/claims.d/CLAIM-298.md) it offers only an analogy (cue-driven matching, the same image read differently by task step) and no test of framing or judgement. |

| [LIT-1181](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1181.md) v2 | Action and behavior: a free-energy formulation | Friston, Daunizeau, Kilner & Kiebel (2010). If an agent's existence requires a low-entropy density over its states, an ergodic assumption makes that entropy the time-average of surprise, and the setup stipulates that only action changes the hidden states the agent senses; so action as well as perception must minimize a free-energy bound on surprise. Action is absent from the generative model and descends on sensory prediction error, so motor control is the fulfilment of proprioceptive (and visual) predictions. Simulations of oculomotor stabilization and prior-driven saccades, cued reaching, a mountain car learned passively in a designed environment, and Lorenz trajectories show unexpected perturbations cancelled by action and not perceived. Synchronous tapping made people rate the touch as produced on the seen arm (13 people), and after onset they went on to rate touch as caused by a finger hovering 5 cm off a rubber arm, or felt on a cardboard box (10 and 11 people); some described the hovering finger as magnetism, ESP or black magic. Nine people shown the box without prior onset gave no synchrony difference. The real hand was 0.13 °C cooler under synchrony in one of four comparisons, by what reads as a one-tailed test. Read it as four small samples, single leading questions with no ownership item, no expectation measure, and a temperature result too weak to carry the claim that the real hand loses ownership. |
| [LIT-1273](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1273.md) | Moving a Rubber Hand that Feels Like Your Own: A Dissociation of Ownership and Agency | Kalckert & Ehrsson (2012), Frontiers in Human Neuroscience 6:40. A moving rubber hand illusion: the participant taps a hidden index finger linked by a rod to the finger of a wooden model hand in view. Synchronous movement gave ownership (mean 1.63 on −3 to +3) and agency (2.44), and a 1.73 cm drift toward the model, where a ~500 ms asynchrony gave neither (n = 20 and 20). In a 2 × 2 design (n = 32 each), passive movement abolished agency (−0.61) but left ownership (1.57) and drift, and a model hand rotated 180° abolished ownership (−0.62) and drift but left agency (2.2): a double dissociation on questionnaires. Agency was higher, and correlated with ownership (r = 0.50), only when the hand was owned. | Active — read 2026-10-20 ([NOTE-993](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-993.md)) in full; worth reading as the first experiment to set the sense of ownership and the sense of agency against each other in one rubber hand paradigm. A wooden model hand whose index finger is linked by a rod to the participant's hidden finger is owned when it moves in time with the real finger, whether the movement is the participant's own or imposed by the experimenter, and is controlled when the participant moves, whether or not it is owned: passive movement removed agency and left ownership, and rotating the model hand 180° removed ownership and left agency. Read it as 104 participants over four between-group experiments, with named non-parametric tests, means and SDs but no standardised effect sizes, a dissociation shown on questionnaires alone (drift measures ownership only), and no control for what participants expected the conditions to do. It also finds the two not independent: agency was rated higher, and correlated with ownership, only when the hand was owned. |
| [LIT-1274](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1274.md) v2 | Full-body illusions and minimal phenomenal selfhood | Blanke & Metzinger (2009), Trends in Cognitive Sciences 13(1):7–13. An opinion piece proposing that research on bodily self-consciousness isolate minimal phenomenal selfhood (MPS), "the conscious experience of being a self", defined by three dimensions: global self-identification with the body, spatiotemporal self-location, and a weak (geometrical) first-person perspective, claimed jointly necessary and sufficient. The rubber-hand illusion and somatoparaphrenia alter only partial ownership and so do not touch MPS; out-of-body experience, heautoscopy and the full-body illusions of Lenggenhager et al. and Ehrsson (2007) do. Agency is causally enabling for MPS but not constitutive of it. | Active — read 2026-10-19 ([NOTE-1002](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1002.md)) in full; worth reading as the short programmatic paper that names minimal phenomenal selfhood (MPS), the simplest form of the experience of being a self, and splits it into three dimensions: self-identification with the body as a whole, self-location, and a weak, purely geometrical first-person perspective. Its distinctive move is to set partial ownership (the rubber-hand illusion, somatoparaphrenia) apart from global ownership, and to say only the second reaches MPS, so that full-body illusions and neurological out-of-body phenomena, not the rubber hand, are the entry point. Its most quotable thesis is that bodily agency "is a causally enabling, but not a constitutive condition, for phenomenal selfhood". An opinion piece: no new data, the evidence cited, and the necessity and sufficiency claims asserted. |
| [LIT-1275](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1275.md) | What is embodiment? A psychometric approach | Longo, Schüür, Kammers, Tsakiris & Haggard (2008), Cognition 107:978–998. 131 participants rated 27 statements after synchronous and asynchronous brushing of a rubber hand. Principal components analysis gave four components in both conditions (embodiment of the rubber hand, loss of own hand, movement, affect) and a fifth, deafference, after asynchrony only. A second analysis split embodiment into ownership, location and agency. Ownership and location were positive after synchronous brushing and negative after asynchronous; agency was negative after both. Drift toward the rubber hand was 1.34 cm after synchrony and a non-significant 0.30 cm after asynchrony, and ownership and location each predicted it. | Active — read 2026-10-20 ([NOTE-1004](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1004.md)) in full, from the published article on the first author's lab site; worth reading as the first large-sample measurement of what the rubber hand illusion feels like, and as the study that split "embodiment" of a rubber hand into ownership, location and agency. 131 people rated 27 statements after 60 s of synchronous and of asynchronous brushing. A principal components analysis found four components in both conditions (embodiment of the rubber hand, loss of own hand, movement, affect) and a fifth, deafference, only after asynchronous brushing. Ownership and location rose above neutral only after synchrony, agency stayed below it, and ownership and location each predicted proprioceptive drift. Read it knowing that the three subcomponents come from a second varimax rotation of ten items dominated by one component, that there is no control for expectation or suggestion, and that every item is about a hand, none about the whole body. |
| [LIT-1277](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1277.md) v4 | Rubber hands 'feel' touch that eyes see | Botvinick & Cohen (1998), Nature 391:756. Ten subjects watched a rubber left hand being brushed in synchrony with their own hidden left hand. After ten minutes they affirmed feeling the touch where they saw the rubber hand touched, that the touch was caused by the brush on the rubber hand, and that the rubber hand was theirs. After a 30-minute exposure, blind reaches toward the real hand were displaced toward the rubber hand in proportion to how long the illusion was reported, and an asynchronously brushed control group reported the illusion for 7% of the time against 42% and showed no drift toward it. The authors conclude that intermodal matching "can be sufficient for self-attribution". | Active — read 2026-10-19 ([NOTE-1006](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1006.md)) in full; worth reading as the one-page report that founded the rubber hand illusion paradigm: synchronous brushing of a seen rubber hand and the hidden real hand makes touch be felt where the rubber hand is touched and the rubber hand be felt as one's own, and after 30 minutes the felt position of the real hand drifts toward the rubber hand in proportion to how long the illusion lasted, while asynchronous brushing abolishes both. Read it as a brief communication: ten subjects, no stated control-group size, statistics given only as P-values, and a connectionist model and a premotor-cell analogy mentioned but not shown. Its closing claim, that intermodal matching "can be sufficient for self-attribution", is the sentence the later literature on body ownership builds on. |
| [LIT-1279](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1279.md) v2 | Video Ergo Sum: Manipulating Bodily Self-Consciousness | Lenggenhager, Tadi, Metzinger & Blanke (2007), Science 317:1096–1099. A whole-body rubber hand illusion in video virtual reality. Participants saw their own back, filmed from 2 m behind, as a body standing in front of them, stroked in or out of time with strokes on their real back. Under synchronous stroking they rated the seen body as theirs and, after blindfolded displacement, returned to a point shifted toward it (24.1 cm in study I, n = 14). In study II (n = 14) a mannequin gave the same, and a non-bodily object a weaker, non-significant drift with no self-identification. Nobody reported disembodiment or a shifted viewpoint. The authors conclude that self-location and the global ownership they tie to selfhood rest partly on the same visuo-tactile integration as body-part ownership, constrained by knowledge of what a body looks like. | Active — read in full 2026-10-19 ([NOTE-999](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-999.md)), with its supporting online material and the 2008 e-letter exchange; worth reading as the first full-body version of the rubber hand illusion and the experiment the self-model theory cites for global body ownership. Two groups of 14 people saw, through a head-mounted display, a video of a body 2 m in front of them being stroked on the back. When the stroking was synchronous with strokes on their own back, they rated the seen body as theirs and, displaced blindfolded, walked back to a spot about 17 to 25 cm toward it. A mannequin worked; a rectangular object weakened the drift and was not felt as one's body. Nobody reported leaving the body or seeing from elsewhere, so the authors call it heautoscopy-like, not an out-of-body experience. Read it as two small samples with modest, partly inconsistent effects, and with a rival reading (self-recognition in a video system) that its critics raised and its design does not exclude. |
| [LIT-1281](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1281.md) | The Rubber Hand Illusion: Feeling of Ownership and Proprioceptive Drift Do Not Go Hand in Hand | Rohde, Di Luca & Ernst (2011), PLoS ONE 6:e21659. Robot arms stroked a rubber hand and the hidden real hand, and felt finger position was probed by a projected dot. Drift toward the rubber hand built up to about 5–6 cm under synchronous stroking, and to the same level when the hand was only seen, unstroked, or when asynchronous stroking was interrupted every 10 s for measurement. Only 120 s of continuous asynchronous stroking held drift near zero (about 1 cm), which reproduces the classic synchronous–asynchronous difference. The questionnaire showed ownership only after synchronous stroking. The authors conclude that drift and ownership come from different integration processes, that asynchrony suppresses drift rather than synchrony causing it, and that drift is not a valid proxy for ownership. Groups were of ten. | Active — read 2026-10-20 ([NOTE-1009](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1009.md)) in full; worth reading as the study that broke the assumed tie between proprioceptive drift and the feeling of owning the rubber hand. With robot-delivered stroking and a visual probe of felt finger position, drift toward the rubber hand appeared under synchronous stroking, under no stroking at all (only seeing the hand), and under asynchronous stroking interrupted every 10 s, at levels not significantly different from synchronous stroking (about 5–6 cm); only continuous asynchronous stroking kept it near zero. Ownership, by questionnaire, needed synchrony. The authors conclude that drift comes from visuo-proprioceptive integration that asynchrony suppresses, and that "conclusions about feelings of ownership cannot be drawn from measuring proprioceptive drift alone". Read it as groups of 10, a visual-judgement measure rather than reaching, and an Experiment 2 whose ownership evidence is anecdotal debriefing, not a questionnaire. |

Gives a probabilistic model for which, in a limiting case, inference and learning "yield exactly the results of SFA", in the way that independent component analysis has a maximum-likelihood reading, and uses the model to motivate several extensions of the algorithm. Not read; this summary is from the abstract. The model's form and the limit taken are not checked here. | Unavailable — registered 2026-10-20, not read. The Wayback Machine reset the connection or returned 429, and the fetch tool cannot reach it. Semantic Scholar returned 429. Title searches found no author-posted copy. So this is a failure on access as much as on availability: a cached copy may exist at CiteSeerX or in the Wayback Machine's capture of Turner's Gatsby page.
