| [LIT-1344](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1344.md) v2 | Neurophenomenal structuralism. A philosophical agenda for a structuralist neuroscience of consciousness | Lyre (2022), Neuroscience of Consciousness niac012. A programmatic paper. Only relational properties cross the neural/non-neural boundary, and spatiotemporal relations, by acquaintance, answer the Newman problem for the brain. Two assumptions: any phenomenal experience is fully individuated, in its specificity, by its place in a quality space (Q-structure); and Q-structure is mirrored by a surjective homomorphism from neural feature maps. With metaphysically necessary supervenience assumed, it argues for reductive physicalism, an instrumentalist structural representationalism, holism about experience (dichromats experience every colour differently) and the actual and nomological impossibility of spectrum inversion. It concerns specific, not generic, consciousness, and denies being a structural realism. | Active — read in full 2026-10-22 ([NOTE-1060](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1060.md)) from the version of record deposited in PubMed Central (PMC9396309, JATS full text via Europe PMC; the OUP PDF returned 403); worth reading as the most explicit statement of phenomenal structuralism as an ontology: each specific phenomenal character is fully individuated by its place in a quality space, that space is mirrored by a surjective homomorphism from neural feature maps, and holism and the impossibility of nomological spectrum inversion follow. It is the statement Negro and Aldé quote as their target. It is programmatic: nothing is tested, the neural half rests on one cited V4 study, it addresses only which experience a conscious state is and not whether it is conscious, and its reduction rests on metaphysically necessary supervenience that the author says he cannot argue for. |
| [LIT-1349](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1349.md) v2 | Report-modulated prefrontal activity and consistent posterior representations during conscious visual perception | He, Zhang, Wang, Meng, Jiang, Xu, Wu, Sheng, Ye & Ding (2026). With report and no-report visual masking and MEG, posterior sensory regions encoded stimulus presence and category whether or not report was required, with stronger alpha-band recurrent coupling for visible stimuli, while prefrontal activity and fronto-posterior connectivity appeared only under report. The authors read this as favouring posterior accounts of phenomenal consciousness. | Unavailable — searched 2026-10-22, no lawful full text reached; it failed on availability. The article is a subscription article in Consciousness and Cognition: Unpaywall reports it closed with no open-access location, OpenAlex lists only the publisher and PubMed, Europe PMC marks it "Subscription required" and it is not in PMC, and Semantic Scholar has no open PDF. No preprint was found on searching Europe PMC's preprint index and OSF preprints by title, or Semantic Scholar by title. The publisher's page (ScienceDirect, PII S1053810026000838) returned 403 to this client. Only the PubMed abstract was read, and the summary agrees with it. No NOTE is filed. A copy from the owner, or from one of the two authors whose addresses PubMed gives (Zheng Ye, Shanghai Jiao Tong University; Xiaobin Ding, Northwest Normal University), would return it to reading. |
| [LIT-1353](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1353.md) v2 | The Theory of Constructed Emotion: More Than a Feeling | Barrett et al. (2025). A reply to van Heijst et al., who proposed that basic emotion theory explains emotions as bodily states and the theory of constructed emotion explains the feelings that arise from them. The authors argue that this split misrepresents constructed emotion through three simplifications, and that the two theories rest on incommensurate assumptions and cannot be reconciled. | Active — read in full 2026-10-22 ([NOTE-1067](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1067.md)) from the publisher's text in PubMed Central (PMC12164598, CC BY-NC 4.0); worth reading as the theory's architects saying plainly that feeling is not a second phenomenon that represents the body's regulation: the same allostatic signals that regulate the body make feeling, an instance of emotion is one whole-brain event, and splitting it into an objective bodily state and a subjective feeling is a premise of basic emotion theory, which they call incommensurable with theirs. It is a reply with no data; its evidence is cited lists, much of it from the authors' own groups, and basic emotion theory is described by its opponents. It does not discuss emotion regulation, reappraisal or therapy. |
| [LIT-1354](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1354.md) v2 | Distilling the Neurophenomenological Signatures of Pure Awareness during Transcendental Meditation | Chandia-Jorquera, van Mil, Estarellas, Dauphin, Pascovich & Canales-Johnson (2026). EEG with retrospective temporal experience tracing in 33 experienced Transcendental Meditation practitioners and 33 sex- and age-matched controls who counted. Practitioners traced higher and more variable "pure awareness" (d = 0.77 and 1.32). A random-forest classifier on distributed EEG patterns separated meditation from counting at 65% balanced accuracy, led by permutation entropy and aperiodic activity, and meditation from rest at 88% sensitivity, led by low-frequency phase coherence. No robust association between the reports and the EEG was found. | Active — read in full 2026-10-22 ([NOTE-1058](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1058.md)) from the bioRxiv preprint, version 3; worth reading as the largest EEG study of Transcendental Meditation with time-resolved reports: 33 practitioners traced more, and more variable, "pure awareness" than 33 matched controls who counted, and a classifier on distributed EEG patterns separated meditation from counting (65% balanced accuracy, on entropy and aperiodic activity) and from rest (88% sensitivity, on low-frequency phase coherence). Its main limit is that the reports were not shown to track any EEG feature. The reports are retrospective ratings on a scale whose top the experimenters defined as "free from content", demand is conceded only for controls, and the study was funded by, and recruited through, the TM organisation. Evidence about a practice period and about reports, not a neural signature of experience with little content. |
| [LIT-1357](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1357.md) v2 | Convergent transcriptomic and connectomic controllers of information integration and its anaesthetic breakdown across mammalian brains | Luppi et al. (2026), Nature Human Behaviour 10(4):777–802. Revised integrated information ΦR, computed pairwise from resting-state fMRI by integrated information decomposition and averaged over region pairs, falls under anaesthesia in humans (sevoflurane, n = 15), macaques, marmosets and mice, with medetomidine–isoflurane in the mouse the exception in the main analysis. It returns on spontaneous recovery in humans, and when central thalamic stimulation restores arousal in two propofol-anaesthetized macaques. Network control energy rises under anaesthesia and correlates negatively with ΦR. Regional ΦR loss is largest in unimodal cortex and follows cortical PVALB expression in human, macaque and mouse. Species-specific mean-field models reproduce the PVALB effect and the advantage of central over ventrolateral thalamic stimulation. The target is behavioural responsiveness. | Active — read in full 2026-10-22 ([NOTE-1064](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1064.md)) from the publisher's open-access version of record (CC BY 4.0); worth reading as the cross-species, causal extension of the same group's synergistic-workspace result ([LIT-949](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-949.md)): pairwise integrated information ΦR from resting fMRI falls under anaesthesia in humans, macaques, marmosets and mice and returns with responsiveness, including when central thalamic stimulation re-awakens two anaesthetized macaques, and it tracks arousal better than the original Φ, causal density or functional connectivity. Its main limit is the target: behavioural responsiveness, which the authors call "presumably consciousness" and an "imperfect marker". It is also pairwise, linear-Gaussian, at rest and content-free, and the causal arm rests on two animals. The PVALB and modelling results are correlational and model-bound. Filed as [THEORY-881](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-881.md). |
| [LIT-1359](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1359.md) v2 | A systems identification approach using Bayes factors to deconstruct the brain bases of emotion regulation | Bo, Kraynak, Kwon, Sun, Gianaros & Wager (2024). Across two fMRI studies (n = 182 and 176), Bayes factors identify four reappraisal-related systems: an anterior prefrontal one selective for reappraisal, a fronto-parietal-insular one engaged by reappraisal and emotion generation alike, a largely subcortical one (amygdala, hypothalamus, periaqueductal gray) active in negative emotion but unaffected by reappraisal, and a posterior cortical one downregulated by it. | Active — read in full 2026-10-22 ([NOTE-1061](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1061.md)) from the bioRxiv preprint, version 2 (10 May 2023), not the closed version of record; worth reading as the first imaging study of reappraisal large enough (n = 182 and 176, replicated in both) to give evidence for nulls, which lets it say which regions are engaged only by regulating, which are shared with generating negative emotion, and which emotion-responsive regions reappraisal leaves unchanged. Most of the reappraisal network is shared with generation, a smaller anterior prefrontal and temporo-parietal set is selective for it, and every subcortical emotion-responsive region, amygdala and PAG included, was unchanged while reported negative affect fell. One instructed strategy, one picture task, BOLD means and one rating per trial; its talk of "subcortical-level affective experience" goes beyond what was measured. |
| [LIT-1362](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1362.md) v2 | Higher-Order Theories of Consciousness (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy) | Carruthers & Gennaro (2001; rev. 2026), SEP. Most kinds of mental state also occur unconsciously (blindsight, absent-minded driving, the agnosic D.F.), and higher-order theories say a state is phenomenally conscious when it is, or is disposed to be, the object of a suitable non-inferential higher-order representation. The entry sets out inner sense, actualist higher-order thought (Rosenthal), dispositionalist dual-content theory (Carruthers) and self-representational and hybrid views (Kriegel, Gennaro, Van Gulick, Picciuto). It gives the objections (targetless representations, the rock, animals and infants, sufficiency, depersonalization) and the evidence and counter-evidence that prefrontal cortex realizes the higher-order states, and concludes no verdict. | Active — read in full 2026-10-22 ([NOTE-1066](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1066.md)) from the live entry, substantive revision of 9 January 2026; worth reading as the map of higher-order theories, which explain what makes a mental state conscious rather than unconscious by a higher-order representation of it: inner sense, actualist and dispositionalist higher-order thought, self-representational and hybrid views, the standing objections (targetless states, the rock, animals and infants, sufficiency) and the prefrontal evidence. Read it knowing that it argues for no verdict, that it is maintained by Gennaro, a higher-order theorist, while Carruthers and Lycan are reported to have given up their versions, and that its empirical section reports results to about 2023 and not the 2025 adversarial-collaboration findings. |
| [LIT-1363](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1363.md) v2 | A beautiful loop: An active inference theory of consciousness | Laukkonen, Friston & Chandaria (2025). Active inference can model consciousness under three conditions: a simulated world model (an epistemic field), inferential competition to enter it (Bayesian binding), and epistemic depth, the recurrent sharing of beliefs by which the world model contains the knowledge that it exists. A hyper-model for precision control is proposed to implement them, and the account is applied to altered states and meditation. | Active — read in full 2026-10-22 ([NOTE-1063](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1063.md)) from the PsyArXiv preprint, version 3 (June 2025); worth reading as the most explicit proposal that what makes inference conscious is recursion over precision: a unified world model, a coherence-driven competition to enter it, and epistemic depth, the model looped back through the hierarchy by a hyper-model that predicts precision at every level, with awareness graded by that depth and not by content. It is the record's best-stated recursive candidate for [QUESTION-254](../../../record/questions.d/QUESTION-254.md). Its main limit is that it is conceptual: no data, no simulation, a formal part (Table 1) that is a standard hierarchy with layer-wise precision hyper-parameters, and a definition of epistemic depth in terms of awareness. A footnote withdraws the claim that meeting the conditions guarantees phenomenal experience. |
| [LIT-1364](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1364.md) v2 | On the minimal theory of consciousness implicit in active inference | Whyte, Corcoran, Robinson, Smith, Moran, Parr, Friston, Seth & Hohwy (2026). Reviewing active inference models of consciousness, it argues that they share a small set of theoretical commitments, which together amount to a minimal and testable theory of consciousness; since all the models minimise the same objective, decomposable into interpretable terms, it can compare phenomena that separate theories treat apart. | Active — read in full 2026-10-22 ([NOTE-1062](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1062.md)) from arXiv:2410.06633v2, the submitted version; worth reading as the clearest statement of the theory of consciousness that active inference models already assume: conscious contents are posterior beliefs about world, body or brain, and a posterior is conscious when it has the capacity to inform discrete, counterfactual policy selection, slowly and precisely enough. It also reviews the simulations of rivalry, access, no-report, interoception, valence and meta-awareness, and names two predictions close to its core. Its main limit is scope: the criterion is one of conscious access, read off models built to report, and the authors hold it only for humans and similar animals. A review with three small simulations of its own; neither prediction is tested. |

On Clive Wearing's repeated claims, in his diary and in speech, that he has just become conscious for the first time, and his denial of earlier awareness when shown evidence of it; the paper weighs whether this is delusion, impaired consciousness or a coping strategy. | Unavailable — no lawful copy reached, 2026-10-22; failed on availability, as far as could be told. | [LIT-1382](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1382.md) v2 | Event perception: A mind-brain perspective | Zacks et al. (2007). Event segmentation theory: perceptual systems continuously predict what will happen next, a transient rise in prediction error is perceived as an event boundary, and boundaries update the event models that guide attention and memory. | Active — read in full 2026-10-22 ([NOTE-1084](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1084.md)) from the author manuscript in PubMed Central (PMC2852534, NIH public access); worth holding as the statement of event segmentation theory: transient rises in perceptual prediction error are perceived as event boundaries and reset working-memory event models, a domain-general mechanism of attention and memory control. A review with mostly correlational evidence; prediction error is not measured in people and the predicted anterior cingulate response at boundaries was not found. A theory of a passive observer of others' activity; it does not mention doorways or one's own intentions. |
| [LIT-1438](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1438.md) v2 | The current status of research on the structure of evaluative space | Norris, Gollan, Berntson & Cacioppo (2010), Biological Psychology 84(3):422–436. A review of the evaluative space model. The affect system has separable positive and negative channels whose joint output is a bipolar predisposition to approach or avoid. They can be activated reciprocally, independently or together. Coactivation, simultaneous or by fast oscillation, is ambivalence, rare and arousing. Asymmetric activation functions give a negativity bias and a positivity offset, and recalibrate with context. Levels of the neuraxis can override one another. Clinical implications for depression and anxiety. | Active — read 2026-10-23 ([NOTE-1101](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1101.md)): in full, from the NIH author manuscript in PubMed Central (PMC2894997, NIHMS165251). Worth reading as the evaluative space model's own later summary, written with Berntson and Cacioppo. Positivity and negativity are separable systems, whose combined output is a bipolar predisposition to approach or withdraw. They can be activated reciprocally, independently or together, and coactivation is ambivalence. Ambivalence and neutrality give the same middling output from different underlying states. Negativity has the higher gain and positivity the higher intercept. It stands in for the unread 1994 and 1997 papers ([LIT-1453](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1453.md), [LIT-1456](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1456.md)). |
| [LIT-1444](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1444.md) | Brain networks subserving functional core processes of emotions identified with componential modeling | Mohammadi, Van De Ville & Vuilleumier (2023), Cerebral Cortex 33:7993–8010. Twenty participants watched 40 film clips during fMRI and rated 119 salient events (12 s each) on 32 CoreGRID features, and heart and respiration rate were recorded. Partial least squares correlation between event-wise brain maps and feature ratings yields six latent variables, the "functional core processes": valuation (wanting-like), novelty, hedonic impact (liking-like), goal monitoring, caring for others ("being moved") and approach/avoidance. No arousal process emerges, and the processes mix components rather than mapping one to one. | Active — read 2026-10-23 ([NOTE-1107](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1107.md)): in full, from the published version (CC BY 4.0) in the Archive ouverte UNIGE (unige:170302). Worth reading as the first attempt to recover the component process model's components from brain and behaviour together. Twenty participants watched 40 film clips during fMRI and then rated 119 salient 12-second events on 32 CoreGRID features. Heart and respiration rate were recorded. Partial least squares correlation found six brain–behaviour latent variables, read as valuation, novelty, hedonic impact, goal monitoring, caring for others and approach/avoidance. For the record, the result is two distinct valence-like networks: a "wanting"-like valuation process and a "liking"-like hedonic one. Each event gets a feature vector, but no within-episode synchronization is computed. |
| [LIT-1452](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1452.md) | Conscious emotional experience emerges as a function of multilevel, appraisal-driven response synchronization | Grandjean, Sander & Scherer (2008), Consciousness and Cognition 17(2):484–495. Componential appraisal models explain feelings better than basic-emotion or dimensional models. Appraisal runs in parallel at sensory-motor, schematic and conceptual levels and stops at the first conclusive result. Consciousness of an emotion emerges when lower levels cannot cope, especially when component synchronization reaches a critical level and duration, so that conscious, representational regulation is required. Conscious feeling needs, besides component synchronization, local and distant neuronal synchronization that integrates the components' representations. | Active — read 2026-10-23 ([NOTE-1115](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1115.md)): in full, from the copy the authors' laboratory (the Geneva E3 Lab) posts on its publications page. Worth reading as the component process model's fullest account of when emotion becomes conscious. Appraisal runs in parallel at several levels and stops when a lower level reaches a conclusive result. Consciousness is recruited when it does not: when component synchronization reaches a critical level and duration that cannot be regulated automatically, so that higher-level regulation, which needs explicit representations, must take over. The feeling is a central representation built by neuronal synchronization, local and distant. Its measures are EEG gamma and beta activity in felt versus unfelt episodes, and phase coherence between brain regions. It partly rivals and partly supports the record's self-model condition for felt valence ([CLAIM-439](../../../record/claims.d/CLAIM-439.md)). |
| [LIT-1455](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1455.md) | Bridging emotion theory and neurobiology through dynamic systems modeling | Lewis (2005), Behavioral and Brain Sciences 28(2):169–194, with open peer commentary. Appraisal and emotion are not cause and effect but constituents that organize one another, through positive and negative feedback and circular causality, into an emotion–appraisal amalgam, an "emotional interpretation". Trigger, self-amplification and self-stabilization phases. Interpretations are attractors, one converging at a time, with abrupt phase transitions between them. Their neural basis is nested corticolimbic loops, neuromodulation, vertical integration, action monitoring and theta-band synchrony, and stable states drive learning on a developmental timescale. | Active — read 2026-10-23 ([NOTE-1119](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1119.md)): the target article in part, from the BBS treatment posted on the University of Geneva E3 Lab's publications page with Sander and Scherer's commentary. Worth reading as the fullest dynamic-systems account of appraisal and emotion. Appraisal and emotion constituents organize each other into one "emotional interpretation" through bidirectional feedback, in trigger, self-amplification and self-stabilization phases. Emotional interpretations are attractors, one at a time, and switch by phase transition. Vertical integration gives them momentum and selects among them. Stable states drive learning across a slower timescale. It contains the dynamics of one organization coming to prevail, but what prevails is an interpretation, not an ordering of the system's own states. |
| [LIT-1459](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1459.md) | Pleasure systems in the brain | Berridge & Kringelbach (2015), Neuron 86(3):646–664. Reward is three separable components: 'liking' (hedonic impact), 'wanting' (incentive salience) and learning. 'Liking' can be measured without report, by orofacial taste reactivity, which is homologous from rats to human infants. It is generated by cubic-millimetre opioid and endocannabinoid hotspots in nucleus accumbens, ventral pallidum and perhaps cortex and pons. Mesolimbic dopamine and most "pleasure electrodes" raise 'wanting' without raising 'liking'. Incentive sensitization makes an addict want a drug that has become less pleasant. Objective 'liking' can occur without any felt pleasure. | Active — read 2026-10-23 ([NOTE-1110](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1110.md)): in full, from the NIH author manuscript in PubMed Central (PMC4425246, NIHMS664561). A review of the affective neuroscience of pleasure. Reward splits into 'liking' (hedonic impact), 'wanting' (incentive salience) and learning, with separable mechanisms. 'Liking' is measured without report by taste reactivity, which is homologous across rats, apes and newborn humans. It is generated by small opioid and endocannabinoid hotspots. Mesolimbic dopamine and most "pleasure electrodes" raise 'wanting' without raising 'liking'. Objective 'liking' can occur without felt pleasure. Filed for the record's account of valence as potential ([CLAIM-440](../../../record/claims.d/CLAIM-440.md)), which wanting-without-liking puts under pressure. |
| [LIT-1461](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1461.md) | Liking, wanting, and the incentive-sensitization theory of addiction | Berridge & Robinson (2016), American Psychologist 71(8):670–679. 'Wanting' (incentive salience, mesolimbic and dopamine-related) and 'liking' (hedonic impact, small opioid and endocannabinoid hotspots) are dissociable. Repeated, especially intermittent high-dose, drug use can sensitize the 'wanting' system, making it hyper-reactive to drug cues and contexts, lastingly and perhaps permanently, while 'liking' need not rise and may fall. Sensitized 'wanting' can oppose cognitive desire, run without report, and grow during abstinence. Its scope is said to extend, on emerging evidence, to behavioural addictions and to the compulsions of dopamine dysregulation syndrome. | Active — read 2026-10-23 ([NOTE-1109](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1109.md)): in full, from the NIH author manuscript in PubMed Central (PMC5171207, NIHMS816820). Worth reading as the authors' own short statement, a quarter-century on, of the incentive-sensitization theory of addiction. Drugs, and perhaps unpredictable non-drug rewards, can make mesolimbic 'wanting' systems lastingly hyper-reactive to cues and contexts, and 'liking' need not rise with it. Sensitized 'wanting' can oppose a person's cognitive desire, operate without report, persist for years and grow during abstinence. It is a review of the authors' programme. Filed for the record's question whether potential of a proxy for maintenance is valence, and the form addiction and metric fixation share ([QUESTION-267](../../../record/questions.d/QUESTION-267.md)), to which it gives a mechanism on the personal side. |
| [LIT-1471](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1471.md) | An Appraisal-Driven Componential Approach to the Emotional Brain | Sander, Grandjean & Scherer (2018), Emotion Review 10:219–231. A perspective article. Major emotion theories agree that emotion has five components, so the emotional brain should be studied as five functionally defined networks: elicitation (appraisal), expression, autonomic reaction, action tendency and feeling. Appraisal drives the changes and the synchronization in the other four. Synchronization is proposed to be neuronal phase or cross-frequency coupling within and between components, and feeling to emerge when it passes a threshold. No measure is given and no data are reported. | Active — read 2026-10-23 ([NOTE-1103](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1103.md)): in full, from the published version deposited in the Archive ouverte UNIGE (unige:109591). Worth reading as the Geneva group's programme statement for taking the component process model into the brain. It splits the emotional brain into five functionally defined networks (elicitation, expression, autonomic reaction, action tendency, feeling). It proposes that component synchronization is neuronal phase or cross-frequency synchronization, within and between components, and repeats Scherer's hypothesis that feeling arises when the degree of synchronization passes a threshold. It names control precedence as priority among action tendencies. It gives no measure of synchronization and reports no data of its own. |
| [LIT-1476](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1476.md) v3 | Active inference and learning | Friston, FitzGerald, Rigoli, Schwartenbeck, O'Doherty & Pezzulo (2016). An active inference account of choice and learning, on how goal-directed and habitual behaviour contextualise each other. Habits emerge naturally from sequential policy optimisation in agents equipped with state-action policies, as learned prior beliefs over policies; epistemic, ambiguity-resolving behaviour enables pragmatic behaviour and then habit. The important distinction is between belief-free and belief-based schemes, not model-free and model-based; the scheme covers dopamine transfer, reversal learning, habit formation and devaluation, and reduces to a Bellman scheme without ambiguity. | Active — read in full 2026-10-24 ([NOTE-1138](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1138.md)) from the CC BY version of record; worth reading as the active inference account in which a habit is one more policy, its transitions and prior probability learned by counting the agent's own behaviour, so that habits form from goal-directed choice and, once formed, survive devaluation. It gives the record a published analogue of a learned log prior beside a precision-weighted evaluation. Simulation of one T-maze task only; its learned prior grows by frequency, not by reward, its reaction times are simulation run times, and the authors concede that it makes probably no new behavioural predictions. |
| [LIT-1494](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1494.md) v3 | Eligibility Traces and Plasticity on Behavioral Time Scales: Experimental Support of NeoHebbian Three-Factor Learning Rules | Gerstner, Lehmann, Liakoni, Corneil & Brea (2018). Behaviour unfolds over seconds and spikes over milliseconds, so learning rules must bridge the two. In neoHebbian three-factor rules, co-activation of pre- and postsynaptic neurons sets an eligibility trace at the synapse, which changes the weight only if a third factor (reward, punishment, surprise or novelty, carried by neuromodulators or special inputs) arrives while it is set. The review sets out four recent experiments supporting eligibility traces on the scale of seconds. | Active — read in full 2026-10-24 ([NOTE-1130](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1130.md)) from the CC BY version of record; worth reading as the review that set out what the first direct experiments (2014–2017) showed about eligibility traces on the scale of seconds: in striatum about 1 s, in cortex 3–10 s with the modulator setting the sign, in hippocampus about 2 s. Mostly slices, one laboratory per region, by theoreticians whose models assumed the traces; they grant that other mechanisms could bridge the same gap, and what is well established is the hour-scale tag of consolidation. |
| [LIT-1680](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1680.md) | Retention of Memory through Metamorphosis: Can a Moth Remember What It Learned As a Caterpillar? | Blackiston, Silva Casey & Weiss (2008). Tobacco hornworm caterpillars (*Manduca sexta*) trained by pairing ethyl acetate with mild shock avoided the odour (78% of 41 fifth instars). Moths that had been trained as fifth instars still avoided it, four to five weeks and a metamorphosis later (77% of 27), and 80% of the tracked moths made the choice they had made as larvae. Odour alone, shock alone and backward pairing had no effect. Caterpillars trained at third instar kept the aversion through two larval molts but lost it as moths. Washing the pupae of trained larvae did not remove the adult aversion, and putting the odour on naive pupae did not create one, so chemical residue on the pupal case does not explain it. The authors suggest, by analogy with *Drosophila*, that the memory survives in mushroom-body neurons that form late in larval life and keep their projections through metamorphosis; they did not examine the brain. | Active — read in full 2026-10-29 ([NOTE-1249](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1249.md)) from the publisher's PDF (PLoS ONE, CC BY), checked against Europe PMC's XML (PMC2248710); worth reading as the clean modern demonstration that a single conditioned aversion survives insect metamorphosis, with contamination controls and a timing dissociation that points to surviving neurons as the carrier; one odour, one lab and adult groups of 15 to 31. |
| [LIT-1707](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1707.md) | The stability of memories during brain remodeling: A perspective | Blackiston, Shomrat & Levin (2015). A perspective gathering three animal systems in which learned behaviour is reported to survive drastic remodelling of the brain: metamorphosing insects, where odour-shock aversions learned by fly and moth larvae persist in adults; planaria, where McConnell's 1960s work and the authors' automated replication report memory surviving head regeneration; and hibernating ground squirrels and marmots, whose hippocampal dendrites are pruned in torpor and regrow on arousal. The authors argue that synaptic plasticity alone cannot explain lifelong memory, propose a "blueprint" kept by another mechanism, and suggest that in planaria memory may be stored outside the brain, possibly in neoblasts or in non-neural bioelectric networks, and imprinted on the regenerating brain. They set out a research programme to test it. No new data. | Active — read in full 2026-10-29 ([NOTE-1258](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1258.md)) from Europe PMC's full-text XML (PMC4802789, CC BY-NC), cited by section; worth reading as the Levin lab's map of the cases and its hypothesis that memory can live outside the brain; a programme, not evidence, which restates its own planarian result in one sentence. |
| [LIT-1732](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1732.md) | An automated training paradigm reveals long-term memory in planaria and its persistence through head regeneration | Shomrat & Levin (2013). With an automated training apparatus, planarian flatworms familiarized with a textured environment fed sooner in it. Worms whose heads were cut off regenerated new heads and, after a brief reminder session, showed the familiarity effect: a memory that outlasts the brain that formed it, perhaps stored elsewhere in the body. | Unavailable — filed 2026-10-29; reading attempted the same day, no lawful copy reached. Unpaywall lists no open copy and a web search found none posted by an author, their institution or the publisher; it is not in PMC. The publisher's pages answered with a Cloudflare challenge, so whether the journal has since opened the article could not be checked, and the Levin lab's publications page links only to the publisher. A copy on a course page was not used. No NOTE is filed. It stays Unavailable until a copy is supplied ([ADR-041](../../../record/decisions.d/ADR-041.md)). Read in its place, and not a substitute for reading it: Levin and Shomrat's 2013 post on The Node (LIT-1776). |
| [LIT-1734](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1734.md) | Mental Hoop Diaries: Emotional Memories of a College Basketball Game in Rival Fans | Botzung et al. (2010). Twenty-three male Duke and UNC fans watched an archived 2001 Duke–UNC game three times in the lab, then under fMRI recalled whether each of 64 shots went in. The same shot was positive for one side and negative for the other, so valence was set by allegiance with the stimulus held fixed. Shots good for one's own team were recalled more accurately and confidently and rated more intense. Emotional intensity, not valence, modulated amygdala, hippocampus, striatum and cortical midline regions; positive shots added dorsal fronto-parietal and sensorimotor activity. Fan groups did not differ in accuracy or intensity. | Active — read in full 2026-10-29 ([NOTE-1313](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1313.md)) from the NIH author manuscript (NIHMS176990, PMC3319676) from the PMC Cloud open-data service, cited by section; worth reading as the one study the record holds in which a fan's allegiance alone decides whether the same remembered play is good or bad, and in which fans remember their own side's successes better; it says nothing about how a rivalry's history is handed on. |
| [LIT-1738](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1738.md) | Molecular insights into transgenerational non-genetic inheritance of acquired behaviours | Bohacek & Mansuy (2015). Reviews rodent evidence that acquired behaviours and stress responses are transmitted through the germline, by sperm RNAs, DNA methylation and chromatin, and what remains open in humans. | Unavailable — filed 2026-10-29; reading attempted the same day, no lawful copy reached. Unpaywall lists no open copy and a web search found none posted by an author, their institution or the publisher. The ETH Research Collection and the Zurich repository (ZORA) list it without a file, as they do Mansuy's other reviews of 2013–2017. No NOTE is filed. It stays Unavailable until a copy is supplied ([ADR-041](../../../record/decisions.d/ADR-041.md)). Read in its place, and not a substitute for reading it: Jawaid and Mansuy 2019 ([LIT-1774](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1774.md)). |
| [LIT-1746](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1746.md) | Parental olfactory experience influences behavior and neural structure in subsequent generations | Dias & Ressler (2014). Male mice fear-conditioned to acetophenone or propanol before mating sired offspring (F1) and grand-offspring (F2) with heightened startle to, and lower detection thresholds for, the odour their F0 father was conditioned to, and not the other one. The offspring of acetophenone-trained males also had more M71 (Olfr151-expressing) olfactory neurons and larger M71 glomeruli; the anatomy, but not behaviour, was also tested and replicated in offspring conceived by IVF and carried by surrogates. Conditioning mothers before mating gave the same behavioural and anatomical effects, which survived cross-fostering. Olfr151 was less methylated in the sperm of conditioned F0 males (n = 12 vs 10) and of their naive F1 sons (n = 4 vs 4), but not in F1 or F2 olfactory epithelium. The authors read the effect as inherited sensitivity to a salient cue, not inherited fear, and leave open how an odour reaches sperm. | Active — read in full 2026-10-29 ([NOTE-1281](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1281.md)) from the authors' accepted manuscript (PMC3923835), served by NCBI's PMC OAI-PMH service; worth reading as the standard animal case for germline transmission of a parent's experience: a specific, double-dissociated effect with IVF and cross-fostering controls, small groups, and a methylation result that is modest, confined to sperm and of unclear unit of analysis. This NOTE does not assess the later critique of the paper. |
| [LIT-1776](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1776.md) | Remembrance of Brains Past | A blog post by the authors of Shomrat and Levin 2013 announcing its result. Planarians trained to a chamber with a rough, laser-etched floor later recognised it, measured by their readiness to eat a piece of liver there rather than explore as naive worms do, and did so again after their heads were cut off and regrown, provided they had "a brief refresher" first. The training used an automated device that gives individual reward and punishment to 12 worms at a time, around the clock, scored by computer, built to answer the doubts about McConnell's hand-run 1960s experiments. The authors conclude that memories "can be stored somewhere outside of the brain" and "imprinted on a naïve regenerated brain", and suggest non-neural cells linked by gap junctions as the store. No numbers, methods or controls are given. | Active — skimmed 2026-10-29 ([NOTE-1283](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1283.md)), in place of [LIT-1732](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1732.md), which could not be reached; worth reading as the authors' own plain statement of the planarian result and of how they read it, including the reminder it needed; too thin to stand for the paper's data. |
| [LIT-1781](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1781.md) | Retention of Learning through Metamorphosis in the Grain Beetle (Tenebrio molitor) | Alloway (1972). Mealworm larvae trained in a maze were reported to relearn it faster as adult beetles, and the paper reviews earlier claims of retention through insect metamorphosis and the difficulty of separating memory from carried-over chemical cues. | Unavailable — filed 2026-10-29; reading attempted the same day, no lawful copy reached. Unpaywall lists no open copy and a web search found none posted by an author, their institution or the publisher. One index marks it open access, but Oxford Academic answered with a Cloudflare challenge, so that could not be checked. No NOTE is filed. It stays Unavailable until a copy is supplied ([ADR-041](../../../record/decisions.d/ADR-041.md)). |
| [LIT-1835](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1835.md) | Binding and Consciousness | Revonsuo & Newman (1999), Consciousness and Cognition 8, 123–127. The editors' introduction to the journal's special issue on binding and consciousness, in which Revonsuo's "Binding and the Phenomenal Unity of Consciousness" ([LIT-1208](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1208.md)) and Engel et al.'s temporal-binding paper appear. Not read: whether it states a functional/phenomenal distinction is the open question it is filed for. | Unfetched — registered 2026-10-29, not read. A lawful free copy is located at an exact address: the Santa Fe Institute wiki, https://wiki.santafe.edu/images/8/8d/Revonsuo_and_Newman_1999_-_Binding_and_Consciousness.pdf, a scholarly third-party copy of the kind the owner's ruling of 2026-10-29 counts. On 2026-10-29 the connection to that host was reset for curl (three attempts, and for the wiki's root page too) and WebFetch got a 503, as on the earlier attempt recorded in [NOTE-1406](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1406.md)'s history. The failure is on access, not availability. OpenAlex reports the work closed with no repository copy; the publisher's page (Academic Press, now Elsevier) is paid. A browser fetch of the wiki copy is the cheapest way to read it. It stays Unfetched until a copy is supplied. |
| [LIT-1946](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1946.md) | Minimal phenomenal experience: Meditation, tonic alertness, and the phenomenology of “pure” consciousness | Metzinger (2020), Philosophy and the Mind Sciences 1(I):7. Proposes minimal phenomenal experience (MPE) as a candidate for the simplest consciousness and the entry point to a "minimal model" explanation. MPE is to lack minimal phenomenal selfhood, time and a spatial frame. Six constraints are drawn from contemplative and Western texts: Wakefulness, Low Complexity, Self-Luminosity, Introspective Availability, Epistemicity and Transparency/Opacity. Sixteen case studies flesh them out. The hypothesis: pure awareness is a temporally thin Bayesian representation of the organism's tonic alertness, a model of an "unpartitioned epistemic space". It "definitely has representational content" and is "non-egoic self-modelling". Tonic alertness without that model, as in unresponsive wakefulness, is not conscious. A conceptual paper. Its evidence is quoted report. | Active — read in full 2026-11-01 ([NOTE-1498](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1498.md)) from the journal's open-access PDF. Worth reading as the founding statement of minimal phenomenal experience, the concept the record's reading of Chandia-Jorquera et al. ([LIT-1354](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1354.md)) takes as given. It holds that pure awareness has representational content: a temporally thin, nonegoic model of the organism's tonic alertness, its "epistemic space". On that account, consciousness without a self-model in the egoic sense still involves self-modelling, and it lacks even a phenomenal quality of oneness. Its evidence is sixteen quoted reports and texts. Its methodological problems, performative self-contradiction among them, are deferred to other papers. |
